blocks.h: 1. What the Internet of Things is

blocks.p: The Internet of Things is the extension of network connectivity to physical objects, so that equipment which formerly only ran can now report on itself and, in some arrangements, be acted upon remotely. The definition that matters for this paper is functional: an IoT system is one in which a physical asset is instrumented, its data is transmitted off the asset, the data is analysed, and the analysis causes an action - a maintenance decision, a load change, a route change, a purchase.

The word to underline is action. A sensor that logs to a local printer is instrumentation, not IoT; a system that measures without changing any decision is a cost with no benefit. At sea, the things are main and auxiliary engines, shafting, boilers, pumps, purifiers, tanks, reefer containers, ballast and cargo systems, the hull itself through its measured performance, and increasingly the crew's own safety equipment.
Every maritime IoT installation, whatever its badge, is the same five layers. Naming them is the cheapest structure in this answer because limbs (a), (b) and (c) can each be hung on them.

ul: Sensing. Transducers for pressure, temperature, vibration, torque, speed, flow, level, position, oil condition and exhaust composition, plus the digital outputs the machinery's own control system already produces. On most ships the majority of the data already exists inside the alarm and monitoring system; the IoT question is whether anything is done with it.

Connectivity. A shipboard network gathering the sensors - fieldbus, industrial Ethernet, and increasingly wireless for retrofit points where cabling is uneconomic - and a ship-to-shore link, in practice satellite, carrying a filtered subset ashore.

Edge processing. Computation done on board, because the satellite link is the scarce resource. The edge device filters, compresses, time-stamps and often does the first level of anomaly detection, so that what is transmitted is a summary and an exception rather than a raw stream.

Analytics and storage. A shore platform holding the fleet's history, where a single ship's behaviour can be compared with her own past and with her sisters. This is where value is actually created, because a reading means little and a trend against a fleet baseline means a great deal.
Application and action. The dashboards, alerts, work orders, charter reports and regulatory returns through which the analysis reaches a human being who can do something.

blocks.p: Two principles cut across all five and are worth a mark each. Interoperability: the value collapses if each maker's equipment speaks only its own protocol, which is why standardised data models matter more than any individual sensor. And security by design: every connection added for monitoring is also a path inward, which is the subject of section 8.

blocks.h: 3. Advantages of loT in the maritime industry

blocks.p: The stem asks for advantages and disadvantages together, so give them as two balanced sets and do not let the first crowd out the second.

ul: Machinery availability rises. Incipient defects are detected as trends long before they reach an alarm setpoint, so a failure that would have been a breakdown becomes a planned intervention in port with the spare already on board.

Maintenance cost falls where it should. Overhauls driven by running hours are replaced by overhauls driven by condition, which removes both the unnecessary opening-up of healthy machinery and the late opening-up of unhealthy machinery.

Fuel and emissions. Continuous measurement of hull and propeller performance, engine load and trim converts fuel saving from an annual estimate into a daily one, and it is the only practical way to manage an operational index that is calculated over a whole year.

Regulatory reporting becomes a by-product. Fuel oil consumption data required under the Data Collection System, and the figures behind the operational carbon intensity rating, come out of the same measurement chain rather than being reconstructed from noon reports at year end.

Shore expertise reaches the ship. The maker's specialist, the superintendent and the class surveyor can see the same data as the Chief Engineer, which shortens diagnosis and reduces the number of attendances that have to be physical.
Safety. Fewer unplanned entries into machinery spaces to investigate a symptom, fewer emergency repairs at sea, and better evidence after an incident.

Commercial and chartering value. Verified performance data settles speed and consumption disputes under a charter party on evidence rather than on assertion, and supports the emissions reporting that lenders and charterers increasingly require.
Fleet learning. A defect found on one ship can be checked for on every sister overnight - something no amount of experience on a single ship can achieve.

blocks.h: 4. Disadvantages, and the ones that are specific to a ship

blocks.p: Divide these deliberately. The first group a ship shares with any industrial plant; the second group is maritime-specific, and it is where the marks are.

ul: Capital and integration cost, and a retrofit is worse than a newbuilding because sensors, cabling and power have to be found in a completed machinery space.

Data quality. A drifting or wrongly sited sensor produces confident nonsense, and the analysis cannot tell the difference. Sensor calibration becomes a maintenance task in its own right - the instrument now needs maintaining as much as the machine.
Alarm and information overload. More data is not more understanding; a system that raises alerts nobody has time to read trains the watchkeeper to ignore it.
Skill and competence gap. The engineer is now expected to interpret trends and statistics, and the training has not generally kept pace with the instrumentation.
Dependence and de-skilling. An engineer who has only ever been told what is wrong may not diagnose it when the system is down.

blocks.p: Now the ship-specific set:

ul: Connectivity is limited, intermittent and expensive. Satellite bandwidth at sea is not shore bandwidth; the architecture has to assume the link will be down, which is why edge processing is not optional.

Cyber security across an OT/IT boundary that used to be an air gap. Machinery control systems were designed when they were unreachable. Connecting them exposes systems with long lives, infrequent patching and safety consequences - the risk is not lost data, it is a lost main engine.

Data ownership and confidentiality. The data describes the owner's ship, the charterer's voyage, the maker's equipment and the crew's actions. Who owns it, who may see it and what it may be used for are contractual questions that are frequently unresolved, and performance data is discoverable in a dispute.
Fragmentation between makers and no single accepted standard, so a mixed-maker engine room can need several parallel systems.
Support at sea. A shore plant with a failed gateway calls the vendor; a ship in mid-ocean cannot, and the ship's staff become the first-line support for equipment they did not specify.
Crew privacy and monitoring. Systems that log actions as well as conditions change the relationship between ship and office, and are resented where the purpose is not explained.

blocks.h: 5. How loT is changing the maritime industry

blocks.p: The stem asks how the industry is changing, so answer with changes and not with a list of gadgets. There are four, and they run outward from the engine room.

From calendar to condition. The oldest change and still the largest. Maintenance, hull cleaning, propeller polishing and even survey are moving from fixed intervals to measured need. It reaches beyond maintenance: a society that accepts continuous monitoring data can allow a machinery planned maintenance scheme in place of the opened-up examination it would otherwise require.

From the ship as an island to the ship as a node. Decisions that were the Master's and the Chief Engineer's alone are now taken jointly with a shore operations centre that can see the same data. This is a real and not always comfortable shift of authority, and the question of where responsibility now sits is one the industry has not fully answered.

From assertion to evidence in commerce. Charter party performance claims, warranty disputes with makers, hull-fouling claims and emissions reporting are all settled increasingly on continuous measured data. New commercial products follow - performance-based charters, and financing whose terms depend on measured emissions.

From periodic compliance to continuous compliance. An annual survey samples a ship's condition on one day. An operational index measured over a whole year, and reported from the same measurement chain, is a different regulatory model - and it is the model the current instruments are moving towards. The examiner will credit the observation that the regulation is what is pulling the technology aboard, not the other way round.

This limb has to be answered against the position at this sitting, and the position is unusually fresh. The 2023 IMO Strategy on Reduction of GHG Emissions from Ships was adopted at MEPC 80 on 7 July 2023 - one month before this paper - and it sets the direction. What is already applicable is more important for an operational answer: EEXI and the operational carbon intensity indicator have applied since 1 January 2023, under MARPOL Annex VI as revised by resolution MEPC.328(76), which entered into force on 1 November 2022. The fuel oil Data Collection System has been reporting since 2019, and SEEMP Part III - the ship's own CII implementation plan - must be on board and kept under review.

That is the pull. EEXI is a design index and is settled once; the CII is an operational rating recalculated every year from how the ship is actually run. It is the operational index that IoT data serves, and the connection is direct: a rating computed over twelve months cannot be managed by looking at it in month twelve.
The measurable levers, and what is sensed for each:

ul: Hull and propeller condition. Shaft torque and speed, speed through water, draught and trim, and weather, reduced continuously to a performance index. A rising power demand at constant speed is fouling, and the system converts a calendar-based cleaning interval into a condition-based one - the single largest controllable operational loss.
Engine condition and load. Cylinder pressure, exhaust temperatures, turbocharger condition and specific fuel consumption against load, so that deterioration is separated from operating point.
Trim and draught optimisation. The measured resistance at different trims for the actual loaded condition, rather than the model-basin curve.
Voyage and weather routing. Speed and route chosen against forecast, with just-in-time arrival where the charter permits it - avoiding the classic waste of steaming hard to wait at anchor.
Auxiliary and hotel load. Continuous electrical load monitoring, which usually finds unnecessary running machinery within days of installation.
Boiler and steam plant, and cargo systems on tankers and gas carriers, where heating policy is frequently more conservative than the cargo requires.

blocks.p: The honest qualification, and it earns a mark: the measurement itself saves nothing. It identifies and quantifies, and the saving is realised only when somebody changes an operating decision, cleans a hull or accepts a slower passage. An IoT installation that is not connected to authority to act is an expensive record of waste.
Place predictive maintenance among its neighbours first, because the distinction is examinable and is often blurred:

ul: Reactive - run to failure. Cheap to plan, expensive when it happens, and unacceptable for anything with a safety or statutory consequence.

Preventive - overhaul at a fixed interval of running hours or calendar time. Safe, simple, and systematically wasteful, because it opens up healthy machinery and can still miss a machine that is failing early.
Predictive - intervene when measured condition and its trend say the machine is deteriorating, at a time chosen for operational convenience. This is what IoT enables.
Prescriptive - the further step, in which the system also recommends the action and its timing. Emerging rather than established at this sitting, and it should be described as such.

blocks.p: The mechanism is a chain of four steps, and it is worth setting out because it shows the examiner that the answer is not a slogan:

ol: Sense the parameters that carry a failure signature - vibration spectra for bearings, gears and imbalance; bearing and exhaust temperatures; lubricating oil condition by elemental analysis, infrared spectroscopy, particle count and base number; cylinder pressure diagrams; motor current signature; acoustic emission; and pressure or flow differentials across filters, coolers and pumps.

Establish a baseline for the individual machine in its own healthy condition and at a defined operating point. Without a baseline there is no such thing as an abnormal reading, which is why the first weeks of any installation produce nothing useful.

Detect the deviation and its rate. The value of the data is almost entirely in the trend: a single lubricating oil result is a data point, and the same result three times with a rising slope is a diagnosis. Compare against the machine's own history, against sister ships, and against the maker's model.

Decide and act. Estimate remaining useful life, generate the work order, order the part, and choose the port. Then feed the outcome back - what was actually found on opening up - because a predictive system that is never corrected by findings degrades into superstition.

blocks.p: Two consequences deserve stating. First, the statutory and class dimension: condition data accepted by the society can support a planned maintenance scheme in place of an opened-up survey, so predictive maintenance is not only a cost measure but a route to a lighter survey burden. Second, the spares and logistics dimension: knowing three weeks in advance which part will be needed converts an emergency airfreight into a routine delivery, and this is often the largest realised saving of all.

blocks.h: 8. What the Chief Engineer has to do about it

blocks.p: Close on the management content, because this is an Engineering Management paper and the examiner wants to see accountability rather than enthusiasm.

ul: Own the data quality. Sensor calibration, correct siting and prompt repair of failed transducers become planned maintenance items. A neglected sensor is worse than no sensor, because it is believed.
Keep the manual competence alive. Indicator cards, sounding rods, feeling a bearing and reading a pressure gauge are the fallback when the system is down, and they are also the check on it.

Treat cyber risk as a management-system obligation, because it is one. Cyber risk has had to be addressed in the safety management system since the first annual verification of the company's Document of Compliance after 1 January 2021, under resolution MSC.428(98), and the guidance is MSC-FAL.1/Circ.3 with its identify, protect, detect, respond and recover elements. In practice: segregate the machinery control network from the business network, control removable media and maker remote access, and know how to run the plant with the link disconnected.
Fix responsibility. Agree in writing what the shore centre may see, what it may advise and what it may not instruct, so that the division of responsibility survives an incident.
Insist that alerts are actionable. Every alert should have an owner and a defined response, and alerts that are routinely ignored should be removed rather than tolerated.
Verify claimed savings against fuel figures the ship itself measures, and record what was found on opening up, so that the system is audited by reality.

blocks.p: End on the proposition that holds the whole question together: IoT does not maintain machinery, save fuel or comply with anything. It converts what the ship already knows into something a person can act on in time - and the value appears only at the moment someone acts.

The stem prints one introduction and three limbs, and the commonest failure is to write a general essay about digitalisation that never separates them. The structure above gives sections 1 and 2 to the introduction the stem expressly asks for, sections 3 and 4 to limb (a), section 5 to limb (b), sections 6 and 7 to limb (c), and section 8 to the management content that lifts the answer out of a technology description. A marker looking for the three limbs can find each of them.

Section 2 is doing more work than it appears to. The five layers are set up once and then reused: the advantages in section 3 are mostly analytics-layer benefits, the ship-specific disadvantages in section 4 are mostly connectivity-layer and security problems, and the predictive chain in section 7 walks the same five layers in order. A candidate who has the layers has a structure for anything the examiner asks about this subject.

Splitting the disadvantages in section 4 into general and ship-specific is deliberate. Every candidate can write cost, training and data overload. The marks separate on bandwidth at sea, the OT/IT boundary that used to be an air gap, data ownership and first-line support in mid-ocean, and putting them under their own sub-heading makes the examiner see them.

ul: Writing a technology catalogue for limb (b). The stem asks how the industry is CHANGING; a list of sensors and platforms does not answer it. Give changes - calendar to condition, island to node, assertion to evidence, periodic to continuous compliance.
Treating IoT and predictive maintenance as the same thing. Predictive maintenance is one application of IoT, and limb (c) also asks about energy efficiency.
Confusing preventive with predictive. Preventive is a fixed interval; predictive is measured condition and trend. This is the single most examinable distinction in limb (c).
Claiming a saving figure. Vendor percentages are not evidence and an examiner may well ask where the number came from.
Forgetting that the measurement saves nothing by itself. The saving comes from the decision the measurement causes, and saying so shows judgement.
Ignoring cyber security, or treating it as an IT matter. It is an ISM safety-management obligation and the consequence is a lost engine, not a lost file.
Importing later law. See the traps below.
Answering as an enthusiast. The paper is Engineering Management and the examiner wants the limitations and the accountability as much as the benefits.

EU ETS did not apply to shipping at this sitting. It applies from 1 January 2024, four months later. Material written for a 2024 sitting of this identical question uses it as its regulatory anchor and it is wrong here.
FuelEU Maritime did not exist at this sitting. Regulation (EU) 2023/1805 was adopted 13 September 2023 - one month after this paper.

The strategy in force is the 2023 Strategy, not the Initial Strategy of 2018. It was adopted on 7 July 2023, one month before this sitting, and it is the freshest thing on the paper. An answer that cites the 2018 Initial Strategy as current is a month out of date.

EEXI and CII are already applicable, not forthcoming. Both have applied since 1 January 2023, so an answer written in the future tense is wrong. The revised Annex VI that carries them entered into force on 1 November 2022 - not 2023.
EEXI is a design index; CII is operational. Expect to be asked which one IoT data actually serves. It is the CII.
Cyber risk in the SMS is not new and not optional. The deadline was the first annual DOC verification after 1 January 2021 and it has passed.
The IACS cyber resilience requirements were future at this sitting, applying to ships contracted for construction on or after 1 January 2024. Do not describe them as applying to your ship.

blocks.p: The route is WHAT - LAYERS - ADVANTAGES - DISADVANTAGES - CHANGES - EFFICIENCY - PREDICTIVE - GOVERNANCE, which maps one-for-one onto introduction, limb (a), limb (b), limb (c) and the close. Inside the layers hold SENSE - CONNECT - EDGE - ANALYSE - ACT. Inside predictive maintenance hold SENSE - BASELINE - DEVIATE - DECIDE, and remember that the fifth step is feeding back what you actually found. Inside the changes hold four FROM/TO pairs. The closing sentence is worth memorising: the value appears only at the moment someone acts.

questions.understand_first: Machinery has always been able to tell you how it is doing - you just had to be standing next to it with a thermometer, a pressure gauge and a hand on the bearing. What has changed is that the equipment can now say it for itself, continuously, to somebody who is not in the engine room and may not be on the ship. That is the whole idea, and everything else follows from it. Once a machine reports on itself all the time, you stop maintaining it on a calendar and start maintaining it on evidence, because you can see it going wrong instead of guessing when it might. Once the office can see the same numbers, decisions that used to be yours alone become shared, which is a real change in who is responsible for what. And once a fuel figure is measured continuously rather than added up at the end of the year, an emissions rule that is calculated over a whole year becomes something you can actually manage rather than something you discover. But notice the two things that are easy to miss. None of this saves anything by itself - the measurement only tells you; the saving happens at the moment a human being changes a decision, cleans a hull or opens a bearing. And every wire you add so the machine can talk outwards is also a way in. Control systems that were safe because nothing could reach them are no longer unreachable, and on a ship the thing at risk is not a file - it is the main engine.

steps.title: What the Internet of Things is
points: A physical asset is instrumented, its data leaves the asset, it is analysed, and the analysis causes an action
The operative word is ACTION - measurement that changes no decision is cost without benefit
On a ship the things are engines, shafting, pumps, tanks, cargo systems and the hull's measured performance
Most of the data already exists inside the alarm and monitoring system

steps.title: The principles - the five layers
points: Sensing - pressure, temperature, vibration, torque, flow, oil condition, plus existing control-system outputs
Connectivity - shipboard network plus a satellite ship-to-shore link carrying a filtered subset
Edge processing on board, because the satellite link is the scarce resource
Analytics and storage ashore, where a ship is compared with her own past and her sisters
Application and action - dashboards, alerts, work orders, regulatory returns
Cutting across all five: interoperability, and security by design

steps.title: Advantages of loT in the maritime industry
points: Availability rises - defects seen as trends before they reach an alarm setpoint
Maintenance cost falls where it should - condition replaces running hours
Fuel and emissions managed daily rather than estimated annually
Regulatory reporting becomes a by-product of the same measurement chain
Shore expertise and class reach the ship without attending
Charter performance disputes settled on evidence; fleet-wide learning overnight

steps.title: Disadvantages, and the ones that are specific to a ship
points: General: capital and integration cost, sensor drift producing confident nonsense, alert overload, skill gap, de-skilling
Ship-specific: bandwidth at sea is limited, intermittent and expensive
Ship-specific: cyber risk across an OT/IT boundary that used to be an air gap - the loss is a main engine, not a file
Ship-specific: data ownership between owner, charterer, maker and crew, and discoverability in a dispute
Ship-specific: maker fragmentation, and the ship's staff as first-line support in mid-ocean
Ship-specific: crew monitoring and privacy

steps.title: How loT is changing the maritime industry
points: From calendar to condition - maintenance, hull cleaning and even survey
From the ship as an island to the ship as a node - a real shift of authority to the shore centre
From assertion to evidence in commerce - charter performance, warranty, emissions reporting
From periodic compliance to continuous compliance
The regulation is pulling the technology aboard, not the other way round

steps.title: loT in energy efficiency optimization
points: The 2023 IMO GHG Strategy was adopted 7 July 2023, one month before this sitting
EEXI and operational CII have applied since 1 January 2023; DCS reporting since 2019; SEEMP Part III on board
EEXI is a design index settled once; the CII is operational and recalculated yearly - the CII is what the data serves
Levers: hull and propeller performance, engine condition and load, trim, routing and just-in-time, auxiliary load, boiler and cargo heating
The measurement saves nothing - the saving appears when a decision changes

steps.title: loT in predictive Maintenance
points: Reactive, preventive, predictive and prescriptive - predictive is measured condition and trend
Sense the parameters that carry a failure signature - vibration, temperature, oil condition, cylinder pressure, differentials
Establish a baseline for the individual machine at a defined operating point
Detect the deviation and its RATE - the value is in the trend, not the reading
Decide, act, and feed back what was actually found on opening up
Condition data can support a planned maintenance scheme in place of an opened-up survey
Knowing the part three weeks early converts emergency airfreight into routine delivery

steps.title: What the Chief Engineer has to do about it
points: Own the data quality - calibration and siting become planned maintenance items
Keep the manual competence alive as fallback and as check
Cyber risk is an SMS obligation - MSC.428(98), first DOC verification after 1 January 2021; MSC-FAL.1/Circ.3
Segregate the machinery network, control removable media and maker remote access, know how to run disconnected
Fix in writing what the shore centre may see, advise and not instruct
Every alert has an owner and a response, or it is removed
Audit claimed savings against the ship's own fuel figures and against what was found on opening up

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the IoT question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 what IoT is; 2 the five layers; 3 advantages; 4 disadvantages, general then ship-specific; 5 how the industry is changing; 6 energy efficiency; 7 predictive maintenance; 8 what the Chief Engineer must do. Sections 1-2 are the introduction the stem asks for, 3-4 are limb (a), 5 is limb (b), 6-7 are limb (c).

retrieval_cards.prompt: Define an IoT system in functional terms, and give the five layers.
retrieval_cards.answer: A system in which a physical asset is instrumented, its data is transmitted off the asset, the data is analysed, and the analysis causes an action. The layers are sensing, connectivity, edge processing, analytics and storage, and application and action. Measurement that changes no decision is not IoT, it is cost.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Preventive or predictive maintenance - what is the difference, and what are the neighbours?
retrieval_cards.answer: Preventive overhauls at a fixed interval of running hours or calendar time; predictive intervenes when measured condition and its trend show deterioration, at a time chosen for convenience. The neighbours are reactive - run to failure - and prescriptive, where the system also recommends the action and its timing. Prescriptive is emerging rather than established.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does sensed data become a maintenance decision?
retrieval_cards.answer: Sense the parameters carrying a failure signature; establish a baseline for that individual machine at a defined operating point; detect the deviation and its rate, because the value is in the trend and not the reading; then estimate remaining life, raise the work order, order the part and choose the port. Finally feed back what was actually found on opening up, or the system degrades into superstition.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which disadvantages of maritime IoT are specific to a ship rather than to any plant?
retrieval_cards.answer: Bandwidth at sea is limited, intermittent and expensive, which is why edge processing is not optional. Cyber risk crosses an OT/IT boundary that used to be an air gap, and the loss is a main engine rather than a file. Data ownership is contested between owner, charterer, maker and crew and is discoverable in a dispute. Makers are fragmented, and the ship's staff are first-line support in mid-ocean.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the regulatory pull behind IoT for energy efficiency at an August 2023 sitting?
retrieval_cards.answer: The 2023 IMO GHG Strategy, MEPC.377(80), adopted 7 July 2023 - one month earlier. EEXI and the operational CII applicable from 1 January 2023 under MARPOL Annex VI as revised by MEPC.328(76), in force 1 November 2022. The fuel oil Data Collection System reporting since 2019, and SEEMP Part III kept on board.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why is EU ETS the wrong answer for the regulatory driver at this sitting?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because it applies to shipping only from 1 January 2024, four months after this paper. FuelEU Maritime is worse still - Regulation (EU) 2023/1805 was adopted 13 September 2023, one month after. The April 2024 sitting of this identical stem rests on both, so circulating material for it is wrong here. Use the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy and the applicable CII instead.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Is cyber risk on a connected ship an IT department problem?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. It has been a safety-management-system obligation since the first annual verification of the company's Document of Compliance after 1 January 2021, under resolution MSC.428(98), with MSC-FAL.1/Circ.3 as guidance. The exposed systems are operational technology with long lives and infrequent patching, so the consequence is a lost main engine, not a lost file.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Does installing an IoT performance system save fuel?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. It identifies and quantifies the loss. The saving is realised only when somebody changes an operating decision, cleans the hull, adjusts the trim or accepts a slower passage. An installation not connected to authority to act is an expensive record of waste - and saying so is what separates a management answer from a technology answer.

blocks.p: A maritime lien is a privileged claim against the vessel herself, arising by operation of law, which travels with the ship into whosoever's hands she passes and which ranks ahead of a registered mortgage. It is not a lien in the ordinary commercial sense at all: there is no possession, no agreement and no registration.
Four features define it, and every later part of this answer is a consequence of one of them.

ol: It attaches to the res, not to a person. The ship is the debtor. The claimant does not have to establish that the owner is solvent, present, or even identifiable.

It arises by operation of law at the moment the claim arises - not by contract and not by registration. It is therefore a secret lien: nothing on the register discloses it, and a purchaser cannot discover it by searching.
It is inchoate until it is enforced. It sleeps with the ship and is crystallised only by an action in rem, arrest and, if security is not put up, forced sale.
It ranks ahead of registered mortgages, which is the feature that makes it commercially significant and which a mortgagee bank has to price.

blocks.p: The justification for so drastic a right is practical, and it is worth one sentence because it explains which claims qualify: the claimants protected are those who could not realistically pursue the owner - a crew paid nothing and put ashore in a foreign port, a salvor who saved the ship, an injured person, a port whose services were consumed. They are given the ship instead of the owner because the owner may be a single-vessel company with no other asset.

blocks.h: 2. How the lien travels with the property

blocks.p: This is the limb the stem singles out, and it should be answered as three propositions and a single exception.

It follows the ship. The lien continues on the vessel notwithstanding any change of ownership, of registration or of flag. A ship sold commercially, re-registered in another State and given a new name carries her liens with her under the new name, and the new owner takes her subject to them. This is the meaning of the expression that the lien travels with the property, and it is also why the technique is sometimes described as the claim following the ship rather than the man.

It binds even a purchaser who knew nothing. Because the lien is secret and unregistered, good faith and absence of notice are no defence. A buyer's only real protections are a warranty and indemnity from the seller, an inspection of the vessel's recent trading and claims history, and - decisively - buying at a court sale rather than privately.

It does not last forever. The lien is extinguished after one year unless, before that year expires, the vessel has been arrested or seized and that has led to a forced sale. For crew claims the period is two years. Time runs continuously, without suspension or interruption, save that any period during which the vessel was under arrest or seizure is excluded. It starts from the claimant's discharge from the vessel for a wages claim and from when the claim arises for the others. Underline continuously: the ordinary rules that stop the clock for infancy, absence or negotiation do not apply, and a claimant who negotiates for thirteen months has lost his lien and kept only an ordinary claim.

The one thing that defeats it is a forced sale by the court. A sale in the exercise of admiralty jurisdiction vests the vessel in the purchaser free from all encumbrances, liens, attachments, registered mortgages and charges of the same nature. The liens are not destroyed - they are transferred to the proceeds of sale, and the fight moves from the ship to the fund. That is the whole commercial point of a judicial sale, and it is why a ship with heavy liens is worth more sold by a court than sold by her owner.

blocks.h: 3. In rem - the action against the ship

blocks.p: An action in rem is an action against the thing. The vessel herself is named as defendant; the writ is served on the ship, physically, and she may be arrested and held by the court. The maritime lien is precisely what gives the right to proceed in rem, and the two ideas are so close that candidates often merge them - but they are not the same, and the distinction is examinable:

ul: Every maritime lien gives a right in rem. Not every right in rem is a maritime lien. Modern statutes also give a statutory right of action in rem for a much longer list of maritime claims - necessaries, towage, repairs, cargo damage, agency. That right is enforceable by arrest, but it does not travel with the ship on a change of ownership and it does not outrank a mortgage. It is a procedural right; the lien is a proprietary one.

Arrest is a means, not an end. The purpose of arrest is almost never to sell the ship. It is to compel security - a P&I club letter of undertaking, a bank guarantee or a payment into court - after which the ship is released and the merits are litigated with the money already secured.
If no security is given, the ship is sold by the court and the proceeds become the fund out of which the claims are settled in the order dealt with below.

blocks.h: 4. In personam - the action against the person

blocks.p: An action in personam is the ordinary action against a person - the owner, the demise charterer, the manager or the operator - leading to a judgment enforceable against that person's assets generally.

Its weakness is exactly the weakness the maritime lien exists to cure. Ships are commonly owned by single-ship companies registered in jurisdictions chosen for that purpose, whose only asset is the ship and which may be wound up the day after the casualty. A judgment in personam against an assetless company is a piece of paper. A claim in rem against the ship reaches a physical asset of real value that must eventually enter some port, wherever the company is registered and whatever has become of it.

In practice the two are frequently pursued together: the action in rem to secure the claim by arrest, and the action in personam to establish liability against a defendant who can be made to pay if the ship's value is insufficient. In India both are exercised by the High Courts in their admiralty jurisdiction, and the statute keeps them separate - one provision governs arrest and the proceeding in rem, another the jurisdiction in personam.

blocks.h: 5. Which convention deals with maritime lien

blocks.p: The International Convention on Maritime Liens and Mortgages, 1993, adopted at Geneva on 6 May 1993 and in force since 5 September 2004. It is the third attempt at the subject, replacing the Brussels Conventions of 1926 and 1967, neither of which achieved wide acceptance - the perennial difficulty being that States could not agree on how long the list of privileged claims should be, since every claim added to it is a claim taken away from the mortgagee.

The 1993 Convention's solution, and the reason it is examinable, is that it fixes a short and closed international list of five liens and then requires that any additional liens a State chooses to recognise under its own law rank after the five and after registered mortgages. The mortgagee therefore knows the worst case.

Say plainly that India is not a party to it. India gives effect to its scheme domestically through the Admiralty (Jurisdiction and Settlement of Maritime Claims) Act, 2017, in force 1 April 2018, which is the statute an Indian candidate is actually governed by. Answering only with the Convention, or presenting the Convention as applying in India, is the commonest error on this question.

blocks.h: 6. The five secured claims, and how they rank among themselves

blocks.p: The Convention secures five claims against the owner, demise charterer, manager or operator of the vessel, and the Indian Act reproduces them in the same order. Learn the order; it is the answer to the last sentence of the stem.

ol: Crew claims - wages and other sums due to the master, officers and other members of the vessel's complement in respect of their employment on the vessel, including costs of repatriation and social insurance contributions payable on their behalf.
Loss of life or personal injury occurring, whether on land or on water, in direct connection with the operation of the vessel.
Salvage - reward for salvage services, including special compensation.
Port, canal and other waterway dues and pilotage dues, and other statutory dues related to the vessel.
Tort claims for loss or damage caused by the operation of the vessel, other than loss or damage to cargo, containers and passengers' effects carried on the vessel.

blocks.p: Three rules govern how these rank against each other and against everything else.

ul: Maritime liens take priority over registered mortgages, hypotheques and charges. This is the central rule of the whole subject.

Salvage jumps the queue. A salvage lien ranks ahead of all liens which attached before the salvage operation, and salvage liens rank among themselves in inverse order of time - the later salvor is paid first. The logic is obvious once stated: without the last salvor there would be no ship to distribute, and nobody would answer a distress call if the reward ranked behind the debts he had just rescued.
Within a category, claims rank equally and abate rateably. Crew claims among themselves, tort claims among themselves - if the fund is short, each is paid the same proportion.

blocks.p: Two categories are excluded from lien protection altogether, and the reason is that they are compensated elsewhere: damage in connection with the carriage of oil or other hazardous and noxious substances by sea for which compensation is payable under any law for the time being in force, and damage arising from the radioactive properties of nuclear fuel, products or waste. Note the drafting - the oil exclusion operates by asking whether compensation is payable under another regime, so it works correctly whatever the state of ratification of the regime in question.

blocks.h: 7. The order of settlement after legal action

blocks.p: This is what the stem finally asks for: once the court has sold the ship, in what order is the fund paid out? Under the Convention's forced-sale scheme it runs as follows, and the sequence is logical rather than arbitrary.

ol: The costs and expenses of the arrest, seizure and sale, and of the upkeep of the vessel and of the crew during that period. These come first for a plain reason: nobody would fund an arrest if the cost of it ranked behind the claims it was funding, and the crew must be fed and repatriated while the ship lies under arrest.
Wreck removal costs, where the national law of the State of forced sale gives them that priority. This is an option States may take; it is not automatic.
The five maritime liens, in the order set out in section 6 above, with the salvage rules applied.
A shipbuilder's or shiprepairer's right of retention, where national law recognises one and the vessel is still in their possession.
Registered mortgages, hypotheques and charges.
All other claims - including any additional maritime liens granted under national law, and the ordinary maritime claims enforced by a statutory right in rem.
Any residue to the owner, which in practice is rare.

blocks.p: And the purchaser takes the vessel free of every one of them. That is the consideration for the whole scheme: the ship is cleaned of her history so that she can be sold for what she is worth, and the claimants fight over the money instead of over the ship.

Because India is not a party to the Convention, close on the statute that actually governs. The Admiralty (Jurisdiction and Settlement of Maritime Claims) Act, 2017, in force 1 April 2018, consolidated the admiralty jurisdiction of the High Courts and repealed the colonial-era enactments that preceded it.

ul: It lists the same five maritime liens in the same order - wages first, then loss of life or personal injury, then salvage, then port, canal, waterway and pilotage dues, then tort excluding cargo and containers.

The lien continues notwithstanding any change of ownership, registration or flag, and is extinguished after one year unless arrest or seizure before that has led to a forced sale by the High Court - two years for crew claims, running from the date the sum falls due.
It commences on discharge for a crew claim and when the claim arises for the rest, and runs continuously without suspension or interruption, excluding time under arrest or seizure.
The same oil, HNS and nuclear exclusions apply.

The order of priority in an admiralty proceeding is three-tier and simpler than the Convention's: first, claims where there is a maritime lien; second, registered mortgages and charges of the same nature; third, all other claims. Within any single category claims rank equally, and claims for various salvages rank in inverse order of time.
On a court sale the vessel vests in the purchaser free from all encumbrances, liens, attachments, registered mortgages and charges of the same nature.
Arrest in rem and jurisdiction in personam are provided for separately, and both are exercised by the High Courts - not by the maritime administration.

blocks.p: Finish on the proposition that makes the whole subject coherent: a maritime lien is the law's answer to a debtor who can disappear but whose ship cannot. Everything else - the secrecy, the travelling with the property, the priority over mortgages, the one-year limit - is a consequence of granting that right and then having to keep it within bounds.

The stem is five questions in one paragraph: what is it, how does it travel, what are in rem and in personam, which convention, and what is the order of settlement. The structure answers them in that order and adds nothing before the first of them, because the marker is looking for five answers and an essay that reaches the convention in the last two lines loses most of them.

Section 1's four numbered features are the load-bearing device. Once they are on the page, section 2 is feature 1 and feature 2 worked out, section 3 is feature 3 worked out, and the priority over mortgages in section 6 is feature 4 restated. A candidate who omits them has to argue each point separately and usually runs out of time.

Keeping the Convention and the Indian Act in separate sections is a deliberate decision and not padding. India is NOT a party to the 1993 Convention. An answer that merges them has told the examiner that the Convention binds India, which it does not, and that is the sort of error that costs more than it looks like it should.

ul: Getting the priority order inverted, with salvage first and wages second. WAGES ARE FIRST. The inverted form has circulated in study material and it is wrong; the statute reads (a) wages, (b) loss of life or personal injury, (c) salvage, (d) dues, (e) tort.
Saying the Convention applies in India. It does not - India is not a party. The Admiralty Act, 2017 gives effect to its scheme domestically.

Treating a maritime lien and a right of action in rem as the same thing. Every lien gives a right in rem; not every right in rem is a lien. The statutory right in rem does not survive a change of ownership and does not outrank a mortgage.
Confusing a maritime lien with a possessory lien. A shiprepairer's lien depends on possession and dies when he gives the ship back; a maritime lien has never involved possession.
Forgetting the two-year period for crew claims, or applying it to all five liens. It is a proviso for the crew claim only.
Saying time is suspended by negotiations. It runs CONTINUOUSLY, and the only exclusion is time under arrest or seizure.
Omitting the costs of arrest and sale from the top of the distribution. They rank ahead of the liens themselves and the answer looks incomplete without them.
Answering the printed 'debtor's claims' literally. What is being settled are the creditors' claims against the debtor's vessel.
Wages rank first, not salvage. This is the single most reliably examined point in the question and it has been published the wrong way round.

But salvage jumps liens that attached before the salvage, and salvages rank among themselves in INVERSE order of time. Both propositions are true at once and the examiner will test whether you can hold them together.
India is not a party to the 1993 Convention. Expect 'so does the Convention bind an Indian court?' It does not; the Act does.
A forced sale by the court is the only thing that cleans the ship. A private sale, a change of flag or a change of name does not. Expect to be asked what a buyer should do about it.
The lien attaches to the ship, not to the owner's fleet. Sister-ship arrest is a feature of the statutory right in rem under national law, not of the maritime lien.
Cargo and container damage is expressly EXCLUDED from the tort lien. Candidates routinely include it because cargo claims are the commonest maritime claims there are.
Oil and HNS damage is excluded where compensation is payable under another regime - because it is compensated there, not because it is unimportant.
The 1993 Convention took eleven years to enter into force - adopted 6 May 1993, in force 5 September 2004. It is a usable example for the entry-into-force question elsewhere on this paper.

blocks.p: The route is WHAT - TRAVELS - IN REM - IN PERSONAM - CONVENTION - FIVE CLAIMS - ORDER - INDIA. For the four features of a lien hold RES - SECRET - INCHOATE - PRIORITY. For the five claims hold WAGES - LIFE - SALVAGE - DUES - TORT, in that order, and remember that cargo is out of the last one. For the distribution hold COSTS FIRST, LIENS, RETENTION, MORTGAGES, THE REST. And hold one sentence verbatim: a maritime lien is the law's answer to a debtor who can disappear but whose ship cannot.

ul: International Convention on Maritime Liens and Mortgages, 1993 - adopted Geneva 6 May 1993, in force 5 September 2004. Successor to the Brussels Conventions of 1926 and 1967. India is not a party.
Convention article 4 - the five secured claims and the oil, HNS and nuclear exclusions.
Convention article 5 - priority over registered mortgages; the inter se order; salvage jumping earlier liens and ranking in inverse order of time.
Convention article 6 - national liens rank after the five and after mortgages.
Convention article 8 - the lien follows the vessel notwithstanding change of ownership, registration or flag.
Convention article 9 - extinction after one year, two years for crew claims.
Convention article 12 - forced sale, the distribution order, and the purchaser's clean title.

Admiralty (Jurisdiction and Settlement of Maritime Claims) Act, 2017 - in force 1 April 2018. Section 8 vesting free of encumbrances; section 9(1) the five liens in order; 9(2) travelling and extinction; 9(3) commencement and continuous running; 9(4) the exclusions; section 10 the three-tier order of claims.
Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 - the general Indian shipping statute at this sitting. It does not govern admiralty priority, which is the 2017 Act's subject.

The Indian half of this answer was read at primary source for this paper. Sections 8, 9 and 10 of the Admiralty Act, 2017 were read verbatim in the MIW corpus, and the priority order given here is the statutory text and not a summary of it.

The 1993 Convention itself is NOT held by the corpus. Its articles are carried from MIW's own verification records, which read the certified text. Nothing here quotes a Convention article, and where the Convention and the Act differ the Act is what is relied on.
The wreck-removal priority is optional under the Convention and is not asserted as Indian law. Whether India has exercised the option is not established from held sources.
No monetary figure or limit appears. Maritime liens are not capped and this question does not reach limitation of liability.
Admiralty jurisdiction is exercised by the High Courts, not by the Directorate General of Shipping. The maritime administration does not appear in this answer at all.

questions.understand_first: Suing somebody is only worth doing if they have something you can take. The trouble with ships is that the company which owns one is very often a company that owns nothing else - formed for that ship, registered somewhere convenient, and quite capable of ceasing to exist the week after the accident. So the law does something unusual: it lets certain claimants proceed against the ship itself, as though the ship were the person who owed the money. The ship can be seized wherever she goes, and if nobody puts up money to get her back, she is sold and the claimants are paid out of the price. The claimants who get this right are not chosen at random. They are the ones who had no realistic way of protecting themselves - a crew left unpaid in a foreign port, someone injured, a salvor who saved her, a port whose services were used up. And because the right is meant to be effective, it has two hard edges. It is invisible: nothing in any register shows it, so a buyer cannot find it by looking. And it stays with the ship, so selling her, renaming her or re-registering her under another flag does not shake it off - the new owner inherits it whether or not he had any way of knowing. Only one thing wipes the slate clean, and that is a sale ordered by a court: the buyer then gets her free of everything, and the arguments move from the ship to the pile of money she fetched. Everything else in this subject is the law keeping so drastic a right within limits - a short list of who qualifies, a queue fixing who is paid first, and a clock that runs out.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the maritime lien question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 what a lien is, in four features; 2 how it travels with the property; 3 in rem; 4 in personam; 5 which convention; 6 the five claims and their internal ranking; 7 the order of settlement after forced sale; 8 the Indian position under the Admiralty Act 2017, kept separate because India is not a party.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Define a maritime lien and give its four defining features.
retrieval_cards.answer: A privileged claim against the vessel herself, arising by operation of law. It attaches to the res and not to a person; it arises at the moment the claim arises without registration, so it is secret; it is inchoate until enforced by an action in rem, arrest and forced sale; and it ranks ahead of registered mortgages. The claimants protected are those who could not realistically pursue the owner.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the five maritime liens in their order of priority.
retrieval_cards.answer: (a) crew wages and other sums due to master, officers and complement, including repatriation costs and social insurance contributions; (b) loss of life or personal injury in direct connection with the operation of the vessel; (c) salvage reward including special compensation; (d) port, canal and other waterway dues and pilotage dues; (e) tort for loss or damage by the operation of the vessel, excluding cargo and containers. Wages first.

retrieval_cards.prompt: In rem or in personam - what is the difference and why bring both?
retrieval_cards.answer: In rem is against the ship herself, which is named as defendant, served physically and may be arrested to compel security. In personam is against a person - owner, demise charterer, manager or operator - and is worthless against a single-ship company with no other assets. Both are commonly brought: in rem to secure the claim, in personam to establish liability if the ship's value is insufficient.

retrieval_cards.prompt: In what order is the fund distributed after a court sells the ship?
retrieval_cards.answer: First the costs and expenses of arrest, seizure and sale and the upkeep of vessel and crew; then wreck removal where national law gives it priority; then the five maritime liens in order; then a shipbuilder's or shiprepairer's right of retention; then registered mortgages and charges; then all other claims; then any residue to the owner. The purchaser takes free of all of it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which convention deals with maritime liens, and does it bind India?
retrieval_cards.answer: The International Convention on Maritime Liens and Mortgages, 1993, adopted at Geneva on 6 May 1993 and in force since 5 September 2004, replacing the Brussels Conventions of 1926 and 1967. India is NOT a party. India gives effect to its scheme through the Admiralty (Jurisdiction and Settlement of Maritime Claims) Act, 2017, in force 1 April 2018, which the High Courts apply.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Does salvage rank first among maritime liens?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. Wages rank first, then loss of life or personal injury, then salvage. The inverted order with salvage first has circulated in study material and is wrong. What is true about salvage is different: a salvage lien ranks ahead of liens that attached BEFORE the salvage operation, and salvage liens rank among themselves in inverse order of time, so the later salvor is paid first.

retrieval_cards.prompt: You buy a ship privately, in good faith, with no notice of any claim. Are you safe from her liens?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. The lien is secret, unregistered and undiscoverable, and it continues notwithstanding change of ownership, registration or flag - good faith is no defence. Only a forced sale in the exercise of admiralty jurisdiction passes clean title, the liens transferring to the proceeds. That is why a court sale can be worth more than a private one.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Is there a maritime lien for cargo damage?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. The tort lien expressly excludes loss or damage to cargo and containers carried on the vessel. Cargo claims are the commonest maritime claims there are, which is exactly why candidates include them by reflex. A cargo claimant still has a statutory right of action in rem and can arrest, but he ranks after the liens and after registered mortgages.

blocks.p: Start here, because all four devices in the stem are doing the same thing and the answer is incoherent without it. A propeller does not convert all the shaft power it absorbs into useful thrust. Two of the losses are physically recoverable, and both of them are left in the water immediately abaft the propeller - which is exactly where the rudder sits.

ul: Rotational or swirl loss. The propeller imparts a tangential velocity to the race as well as an axial one. That rotating column of water carries real kinetic energy which does nothing for the ship, and it is typically the largest single recoverable loss - of the order of several per cent of delivered power on a conventional single-screw ship.

The hub vortex. Behind the propeller boss there is a low-pressure core into which a concentrated vortex forms. It costs drag, it is a source of cavitation erosion and pressure pulses, and it is entirely wasteful.
Separation and drag on the rudder itself. Not a propeller loss at all, but a loss the rudder introduces - and one that can be reduced by shaping the rudder correctly for the flow it actually meets.

blocks.p: The rudder is the only large appendage standing in the accelerated, swirling slipstream, and it is already there, already structurally supported and already surveyed. That is why so much energy-saving effort has been directed at it. State plainly what follows: a rudder device recovers energy that is already being wasted. It does not create thrust from nothing, and its gain is therefore bounded by the size of the loss it is recovering from.

What it is. A pair of horizontal, wing-like fins projecting from each side of the rudder, set within the propeller slipstream, usually one pair above and one pair below the shaft line, and generally close to the leading edge.

How it works. The flow arriving at the fin is not axial - it carries the propeller's swirl, and above the shaft line the tangential component is in one direction while below it the direction is reversed. Each fin is therefore set at a small angle of attack to its own local flow, and as an aerofoil it develops lift. Because the fin is horizontal, the lift vector is roughly athwartships and its resolved component points forward - that forward component is recovered thrust. Simultaneously the fin straightens the swirl it has taken energy out of, which reduces the residual rotational loss further aft.

Practical points that earn marks. The fins are handed: because the swirl reverses across the shaft line, the upper and lower fins are set at opposite angles, and a fin fitted the wrong way up is a drag device. They are usually combined with a rudder bulb, which carries the fin roots and gives them a sound structural attachment. They add wetted surface and therefore some frictional drag, so the net gain is the recovered thrust minus that penalty. Claimed gains are of the order of 2 to 5 per cent at design condition.

Limitations. The gain falls away off the design draught and speed, because the swirl field and the fin's angle of attack both change. In heavy weather and astern running the fins are loaded in ways they were not optimised for, and their attachment to the rudder must be designed for it.

What it is. A rudder whose section is not the same above and below the propeller shaft line - either twisted, so that the leading edge is turned one way above the shaft and the other way below it, or offset, with the two halves displaced relative to the centreline.

How it works. The reasoning follows directly from section 1. Above the shaft line the swirling race approaches the rudder from one side; below it, from the other. A conventional symmetrical rudder set on the centreline therefore meets an incident angle of attack over almost its entire span, even with the helm amidships. The consequences are continuous lift-induced drag, flow separation, and - most importantly on a modern high-power ship - cavitation on the rudder surface, particularly at the leading edge and around the gap at the horn.

Twisting the leading edge so that each half is aligned with its own local inflow removes the built-in incidence. The result is less separation, less drag, and a rudder that is working with the flow rather than against it. Course-keeping usually improves as well, because the rudder is no longer generating a small standing side force that the helmsman or autopilot must trim out.

Practical points. The twist is designed for one propeller, one direction of rotation and one loading condition, so an asymmetric rudder is not a general-purpose component and cannot simply be transferred between ships. It is frequently combined with a leading-edge bulb and with fins, the three being designed together. It is a newbuilding or major-conversion item rather than a bolt-on retrofit, because the rudder itself is replaced. Claimed gains are of the order of 2 to 6 per cent, and on many installations the cavitation and erosion benefit is the real one - a rudder that stops eroding saves steel repairs and off-hire whether or not the fuel saving is realised.

What it is. A streamlined, roughly axisymmetric body fitted on the leading edge of the rudder, aligned with and close abaft the propeller boss, so that boss and bulb together form a continuous faired body.

How it works. It attacks the hub vortex specifically. The propeller boss ends abruptly, the flow cannot close behind it, and a low-pressure core forms in which the hub vortex is generated. Placing a bulb in that space fills the volume the vortex would occupy and allows the flow to close gradually along a fair body instead of separating. The vortex is suppressed or greatly weakened, and with it go the vortex drag, a source of cavitation erosion on the rudder, and part of the pressure-pulse excitation transmitted into the hull.

Practical points. The gap between boss and bulb, and the alignment, are critical - a bulb that is too far aft or off the shaft axis achieves very little, and the installation tolerance is a real construction issue. The bulb is very commonly the structural base for thrust fins, and the combined arrangement is what most makers actually supply. It is one of the more practicable retrofits, because it can often be added to an existing rudder in dry dock without replacing it. Claimed gains are of the order of 2 to 5 per cent, and are larger on heavily loaded propellers, where the hub vortex is strongest - which also means the benefit is greatest on exactly the ships that suffer most from rudder erosion.

What it is. A freely rotating wheel of larger diameter than the propeller, mounted on the propeller shaft or on its own bearing immediately abaft the propeller, and connected to nothing. It absorbs no shaft power at all.

How it works. This is the most elegant idea of the four and it should be explained in two parts, because the whole device turns on the fact that its blades do two different jobs at two different radii.

ul: The inner portion of the span lies inside the propeller race. There the swirling, accelerated flow drives the blade section round - the wheel is acting as a turbine, extracting rotational energy from the slipstream and using it to spin itself.
The outer portion of the span lies outside the race, in undisturbed water. There the same rotation makes the blade section act as a propeller, generating additional thrust.

The wheel therefore takes wasted rotational energy from the race and converts it into axial thrust in the surrounding water, taking nothing from the engine. It free-wheels at a speed set by the balance between the turbine torque inboard and the propeller torque outboard.

blocks.p: Why it is treated differently from the other three. The stem asks about devices currently in use, and an honest answer distinguishes here. Claimed gains reached about 10 per cent, the highest of any device in this family, and a number of ships were fitted in the 1980s. Service experience was poor. The outer blade span is long, slender and lightly supported, and it runs in a highly unsteady flow at the boundary between the race and the free stream; blade fatigue and blade loss were experienced, along with bearing problems on the free-running hub. A lost blade means severe imbalance on an unrestrained wheel immediately abaft the propeller. The device is consequently rare in service today, and is examined mainly because it demonstrates the principle in its purest form.

blocks.h: 6. What the four have in common, and how they combine

blocks.p: Pull the four together before moving on, because this is where a candidate demonstrates understanding rather than recall.

ul: All four are recovery devices, not power sources. Each takes energy that is already in the water and turns some of it into thrust or removes a drag penalty. None improves the engine, the shafting or the propeller itself.

Three of the four attack rotational energy - fins, twist and the vane wheel all work on the swirl. Only the bulb attacks a different loss, the hub vortex, which is why the bulb combines so well with the others.

The gains do not add. This is the single most important qualification in the answer. A bulb, a pair of fins and a twisted section are all drawing on the same finite pool of wasted energy, so fitting all three does not give the sum of their individually claimed percentages. The combined arrangement must be designed and tested as one system.

They are propeller-and-hull specific. Every one of them is optimised for a particular wake field, propeller, direction of rotation, draught and speed. A device transferred from a sister ship in a different trade will not perform as advertised.

They are permanent appendages with structural and survey consequences. Attachment, welding, fatigue and inspection access have to be considered, and the fitting is examined at the ship's underwater surveys.

blocks.p: For completeness in one sentence, so the examiner sees the boundary: the propeller-side members of the same family - ducts, boss cap fins and pre-swirl stators - attack the same losses from ahead of or on the propeller, and the stem confines this answer to the rudder side.
The stem is set in an Engineering Management paper, so say how the choice is actually made.

ul: Retrofit feasibility. A bulb, and fins on a bulb, are realistic retrofits in a scheduled dry docking. An asymmetric rudder generally is not, because the rudder is replaced; it belongs to a newbuilding or a major conversion.

Operating profile, not design point. The device is optimised at a draught and speed. Judge it against the ship's actual laden and ballast draughts and her actual service speed, which after years of slow steaming is frequently well below the design point at which the gain was calculated.

Do the cheap things first. A fouled hull or a rough, pitted propeller will erase the entire gain of any of these devices, and hull and propeller cleaning costs a fraction of a retrofit. It is difficult to justify an energy saving device on a ship whose hull performance is not already being managed.

Commercial and regulatory driver. At this sitting the pressure is real and current: EEXI and the operational carbon intensity rating have applied since 1 January 2023, and the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy was adopted on 7 July 2023, one month before this examination. A device that improves the attained EEXI or the annual rating has a value beyond the fuel bill.

Structural and class approval. The attachment, the local scantlings and the fatigue assessment need the society's approval, and the rudder's cavitation behaviour after modification should be assessed rather than assumed.
Docking and inspection. Fins and bulbs are exposed appendages. They are damaged by ice, by tugs and by contact, and their condition is a docking survey item.

blocks.h: 8. Judging whether a claimed gain is real

blocks.p: Close on the critical judgement, because this is what separates an engineer's answer from a brochure.

ul: Quoted percentages are almost always model-scale or computational results at the design condition - design draught, design trim, design speed, calm water, clean hull.

Scale effects flatter the model. The wake field and the boundary layer of a model do not scale exactly to full size, and energy saving devices working in the wake are precisely where that error is largest.
The gains of combined devices are not additive, for the reason given in section 6.
The ship rarely operates at the design point. Trim, draught, fouling, weather and part-load running all move her away from it.

Verify in service by measurement, not by assertion. The route is continuous hull and propeller performance monitoring - shaft power against speed through water, corrected for displacement, trim and weather - assessed on the industry standard for measuring changes in hull and propeller performance, ISO 19030, over enough time to separate the device's effect from fouling.
Ask for full-scale before-and-after data from a sister ship in a comparable trade, and treat a maker unable to supply it accordingly.

blocks.p: End on the proposition that governs the whole subject: these devices do not make the ship more powerful - they make her waste less. The gain is bounded by the loss, it is largest where the loss is largest, and it is real only if it can still be measured on the ship a year later.

The stem names four devices and invites four disconnected descriptions. The structure above refuses that: section 1 establishes the two recoverable losses first, and then each device is explained as an attack on one of them. The payoff is visible in section 6 - the candidate can say why the gains do not add, which is a proposition he cannot reach at all if he has described four devices in isolation.

Sections 2 to 5 are deliberately parallel - what it is, how it works, practical points, limitations - so the marker can find each device instantly and so the candidate has a template he can apply under time pressure to a device he half remembers. The parallel structure is also insurance: if time runs short, the last device still gets its two most valuable sentences.

Sections 7 and 8 are what lift this from a naval-architecture answer to an Engineering Management answer. ul: Describing four devices without ever saying what energy they are recovering. The loss budget is the answer's spine and without it nothing else can be justified.
Adding the claimed percentages together. A bulb at 4 per cent plus fins at 4 per cent plus a twisted section at 4 per cent is not 12 per cent - all three are drawing on the same wasted energy.
Quoting percentages as though they were measured in service. They are model-scale or CFD figures at the design point and should be labelled as claims.

Getting the thrust fin mechanism wrong. The fin is HORIZONTAL, generates lift because the swirling flow meets it at an angle, and the FORWARD component of that lift is the recovered thrust. Fins are handed and set at opposite angles above and below the shaft line.
Saying an asymmetric rudder is asymmetric port-and-starboard for steering. It is asymmetric ABOVE AND BELOW the shaft line, because that is where the swirl reverses.
Presenting the Grim vane wheel as current equipment. The stem says 'currently in use' and honesty about its service record is worth more than pretending.
Forgetting that a fouled hull or a rough propeller erases the whole gain. Maintenance is the first energy saving measure.
Citing the 2018 Initial Strategy as the current IMO strategy. See the traps.

The operative IMO strategy at this sitting is the 2023 Strategy, MEPC.377(80), adopted 7 July 2023 - one month before this paper. The Initial Strategy of 2018 has been superseded. Note the direction of this trap: it is not a later paper importing later law, it is an EARLIER sitting of the identical question whose correct citation has gone stale in the seven months between January and August 2023.
EEXI and the operational CII are already applicable, not forthcoming - both since 1 January 2023. The revised Annex VI that carries them entered into force 1 November 2022.
The swirl reverses across the shaft line. Expect to be asked why the upper and lower fins are set at opposite angles. If they were set the same way, one pair would be a drag device.

The rudder bulb attacks a DIFFERENT loss from the other three. Fins, twist and the vane wheel all work on rotational energy; the bulb works on the hub vortex. That is why the bulb combines with the others and why they compete with each other.
The vane wheel takes no power from the engine. Expect 'where does its energy come from?' From the wasted rotational energy in the race, which drives the inner span as a turbine.
An asymmetric rudder is designed for one propeller and one direction of rotation. Expect to be asked whether you could fit the sister ship's rudder. Not if she turns the other way.
The cavitation benefit is often the real benefit. A rudder that stops eroding saves steel and off-hire whether or not the fuel saving materialises - and saying so is a mark for judgement.
